Consult Summary:
- 40-year-old female with 3 days of watery then very loose diarrhoea, associated with vomiting and subjective high temperature; periumbilical abdominal pain and decreased oral intake.
- Clinician impression: likely infectious gastroenteritis (probable viral); plan urgent clinic appointment for stool sample and hydration assessment; advised continued small sips of oral rehydration solution and A&E if worsening.

Problem List:

Issue 1: Acute diarrhoea and vomiting (presumed infectious gastroenteritis)
- Timeline and symptoms:
  - Diarrhoea began 3 days ago, initially watery then very loose; patient has had at least four bowel movements today and "lost count" overall.
  - Vomiting started this morning after breakfast; patient reports inability to keep down liquids (water, tea, ORS).
  - Subjective high temperature ("literally boiling") — no thermometer reading available.
  - Periumbilical abdominal pain, intermittent, severe to touch; associated with urgent need to defecate when pain occurs.
- Systems review / pertinent positives and negatives:
  - Positive: diarrhoea, vomiting, abdominal pain, subjective fever.
  - Negative: no blood in stool or urine reported, no rash.
- Social / exposure history:
  - Close contact with brother who has similar symptoms; brother reports this is widespread at school.
- Medications and self-treatment:
  - Oral rehydration solution (salt-sugar ORS) taken ~3 times daily for past 2 days but vomited and reports limited benefit.
- Examination findings (patient-reported):
  - Tenderness around the navel area; passed urine approximately one hour prior to consult (suggests some ongoing urine output).
- Specialist/allied health/differential:
  - Clinician impression: likely infectious gastroenteritis, commonly viral; stool sample recommended to exclude bacterial pathogen.

Issue 2:
- No other active complaints reported during this consult.
- Menstrual history: last period 2 weeks ago; occasional menstrual cramps managed with ibuprofen as needed.
- No other medical or surgical problems reported.

Issue 3:
- No additional issues raised.
- Routine bowel habits: normally one daily bowel movement; no history of chronic diarrhoea or constipation.

Medications:
- Vitamin D — dose/route/frequency not documented (reports daily).
- Oral rehydration solution (ORS) — dose/route/frequency not fully documented (patient reports ~3 times daily for past 2 days).
- Ibuprofen as needed for menstrual cramps — dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
- Not documented in the transcript.

Past Medical History:
- No chronic medical conditions reported.
- Occasional menstrual cramps; otherwise normal past health as reported.

Social History:
- Lives with brother and mother.
- Occupation: graphic designer; working from home today due to illness.
- Smoking: denies smoking.
- Alcohol: occasional — "a pint from time to time."
- Recreational drugs: denies.
- Sexual activity: not currently having regular sexual intercourse; not using contraception.

Preventative History:
- No preventative care details documented (cervical screening, mammogram, PSA, FOBT, BMD, vaccinations, optometry, skin checks not mentioned).

Physical Examination:
- No formal vital signs recorded in transcript.
- Patient-reported findings only:
  - Subjective fever (patient feels "roasting"); no thermometer measurement.
  - Periumbilical abdominal tenderness; unable to tolerate palpation at navel.
  - Passed urine ~1 hour before consult; urine color not assessed.

Plan:
- Actions advised and arranged:
  - Urgent appointment to be arranged at clinic to assess hydration and obtain stool sample for microbiological testing.
  - Continue oral rehydration solution in very small, frequent sips to minimize vomiting.
  - Advise small, bland foods if tolerated (toast/biscuits); avoid fruit, vegetables, milk while symptomatic.
  - If symptoms worsen, significant inability to maintain fluids, or other red flags, attend A&E urgently.
  - Patient to contact service/support line to book urgent clinic appointment; clinician or service to arrange booking (patient asked clinician to book via support line).
- Further follow-up:
  - Clinic will assess hydration status and send stool sample for analysis; further management (including possible antimicrobial therapy) will depend on results and clinical assessment.
  - Patient instructed to call back or present to A&E if deteriorating.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - No objective vital signs (temperature, heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation).
  - No formal assessment of hydration status (capillary refill, mucous membranes, skin turgor, urine output quantification).
  - No stool sample collected during the call (appointment requested).
  - No laboratory tests or pregnancy test documented.
  - No documented allergies or medication reconciliation beyond patient report.
  - Medication doses/routes/frequencies not documented for vitamin D and ibuprofen; ORS frequency approximate.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - None identified.
- Transcript quality:
  - Generally clear audio and content; some brief pauses and incomplete responses (e.g., address and some prompts) but clinically relevant information was intelligible.
